stem:
A school near Bulawayo reared a batch of broilers. A sample of birds was weighed each week.

| Age (weeks) | Mean live mass (kg) |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.045 |
| 1 | 0.170 |
| 2 | 0.450 |
| 3 | 0.880 |
| 4 | 1.400 |
| 5 | 1.950 |
| 6 | 2.445 |

Each bird ate 4.08 kg of feed from hatching to six weeks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the type of feed given to the broilers in their first week.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean live-weight gain per bird from week 0 to week 6, in kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the feed conversion ratio, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: In which week did the birds gain the most mass?

options.content: Week 0 to week 1, when the chicks were growing fastest of all

parts.explanation: Weekly gains: 0.125, 0.28, 0.43, 0.52, 0.55, 0.495 kg; the largest is from week 4 to week 5.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why a low feed conversion ratio is important to a broiler farmer.

points.description: Less feed is needed for each kilogram of live-weight gain.
Feed is the largest cost, so a low FCR reduces costs and increases profit.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** ways of improving the feed conversion ratio of the next batch.

points.description: Keep the brooder at the correct temperature, so feed energy is not used to keep warm.
Set feeders at back height and avoid spillage/wastage; keep rats out.
Prevent disease (vaccination, dry litter, hygiene) and sell at the right age before FCR worsens.

explanation: Broiler growth data, gain and FCR, and how management affects feed efficiency.

stem: A described diagram of the stomach of a cow shows four compartments: W, the largest, on the left side of the abdomen; X, a small compartment with a honeycomb lining; Y, a compartment with many leaf-like folds; Z, a compartment with glands in its wall that leads to the small intestine.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name compartment X.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name compartment Z.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: In which compartment is most cellulose broken down by microbes?

options.rationale: The reticulum is small and mainly moves food and traps heavy objects.
The abomasum digests with gastric juice, not microbes.

parts.explanation: W, the rumen, is the fermentation chamber.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: In this cow W holds 135 L and the whole stomach holds 180 L. Calculate W as a percentage of the whole stomach.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** products of microbial fermentation in compartment W.

points.description: Volatile fatty acids (absorbed for energy).
Methane / carbon dioxide / microbial protein / B vitamins.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain how rumination helps the cow digest roughage.

points.description: The cud is regurgitated and chewed again, breaking fibre into smaller pieces with a larger surface area for microbes.
Chewing produces much saliva that buffers (neutralises) the acids in the rumen.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Explain why a pig cannot live on grass as a cow can.

points.description: The pig has a simple stomach with no rumen, so it has few microbes to digest cellulose.
So it gets little energy from grass and needs concentrates rich in starch and protein.

explanation: Identify ruminant stomach compartments and link structure to function and diet.
hints: The order is rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum.

stem:
Form 4 pupils slaughtered and dressed a broiler and a rabbit and weighed them.

| Animal | Live mass (kg) | Dressed carcass (kg) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broiler | 2.10 | 1.512 |
| Rabbit | 2.50 | 1.35 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the dressing percentage of the broiler.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the dressing percentage of the rabbit.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which statement best explains why the rabbit has the lower dressing percentage?

options.content: Rabbit meat is heavier than chicken meat
options.rationale: This would raise, not lower, the percentage.

options.content: The rabbit was not bled after slaughter
options.rationale: Proper dressing includes bleeding; this is not the explanation.

options.content: Feathers are left on the broiler carcass when it is weighed
options.rationale: Feathers are removed from a dressed broiler.

options.content: Its pelt and its large digestive tract are removed
options.rationale: Correct: the skin and a large gut (with the caecum) are a big share of a rabbit's live mass.

parts.explanation: Rabbits lose the pelt, head, feet and a large gut, so a smaller share of live mass remains as carcass.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why feed is withdrawn for some hours before slaughter, but water is not.

points.description: An empty gut makes evisceration cleaner and reduces contamination of the carcass.
Water prevents dehydration / stress and loss of carcass mass and quality.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Describe how the rabbit's pelt should be prepared for sale.

points.description: Remove the skin whole (cased) by peeling it from the hind legs downwards.
Scrape off fat and flesh and stretch it flesh-side out on a wire or board stretcher.
Dry it in the shade (not in hot sun) and store it dry, away from insects.

explanation: Dressing percentages of a broiler and a rabbit, slaughter preparation and pelts.

stem: A described diagram of the reproductive system of a cow lists, from the inside: P, two oval organs; Q, two narrow tubes with funnel-shaped ends; R, a body with two horns; S, a thick, muscular neck; T, a passage; U, the external opening. The cow was served by a bull on 14 April 2026.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the part, by letter or name, in which fertilisation takes place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name part S.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State the cow's expected calving date, using a gestation period of 283 days.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Before service, which sign best showed that the cow was on heat?

options.content: She stood still when other cows mounted her
She lay quietly apart from the herd all day
Her appetite increased and she grazed for longer than usual

parts.explanation: Standing to be mounted is the surest sign of heat.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** functions of part P.

points.description: Produces eggs (ova).
Produces hormones (oestrogen and progesterone) / forms the corpus luteum that maintains pregnancy.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe what happens from fertilisation until the embryo is attached in part R.

points.description: A sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus in the oviduct to form a zygote.
The zygote divides repeatedly into an embryo as it moves down the oviduct to the uterus.
The embryo implants in the uterus wall and a placenta forms, through which it gets food and oxygen.

explanation: Identify parts of the cow's reproductive system, predict calving and describe fertilisation.
hints: Order: ovaries, oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina, vulva.
Gestation of a cow is about 283 days.
